This presentation summarises the technical report. The focus is not only on dashboard-style reporting, but on using visual analytics to discover distributional patterns and potential drivers of profitability and volatility.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
Analytical objective

Explore numerical and categorical distributions.
Investigate factors associated with profitability.
Use visual evidence and statistical validation together.
Treat extreme losses as part of volatility, not noise to ignore.


The assignment asks for both univariate and bivariate visual analytics. I define profitability through profit and loss ratio, and volatility through spread, claim occurrence, and extreme incurred-loss behaviour.

Data: large policy-year portfolio from Mendeley motor insurance data.

The dataset is large enough for both descriptive and statistical analysis. I use reproducible R code so the results can be regenerated from the raw Mendeley files.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
Portfolio trend


Premium and incurred losses both increased over time.
Incurred loss growth needs to be compared against premium growth.


Premium and incurred losses both increase from 2022 to 2024. The key question is whether premium growth is sufficient to absorb the increasing loss burden.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
Loss ratio worsened in 2024


2024 has a visibly higher aggregate loss ratio.
This suggests weaker underwriting profitability before expenses.


The 2024 loss ratio is visibly higher than 2022 and 2023. This points to declining profitability, assuming expenses are not separately modelled here.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
Univariate: numerical skewness


Numerical variables are strongly right-skewed.
Most records have no incurred loss, but a small upper tail is material.


The most important univariate pattern is claim zero-inflation and right skewness. Many records have no incurred loss, but a small number of records have very large loss ratios.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
Univariate: categorical concentration


Portfolio mix is concentrated in selected policy and bonus-score categories.
High loss ratios should be read together with exposure size.


Policy mix and bonus-score mix are concentrated. This affects interpretation: a smaller category can have a high loss ratio, but it must be evaluated against exposure size.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
Policy type and profitability


Comprehensive products have the highest aggregate loss ratios.
COMP_N is the main policy type requiring closer review.


Comprehensive products, especially COMP_N, have the highest aggregate loss ratios. Third-party-only coverage has the lowest ratio in this comparison.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
Volatility by policy type


Capped boxplots reveal spread without extreme outliers dominating the view.
Volatility is mainly driven by right-tail policy-year losses.


The boxplot uses capped loss ratio to make the spread visible. The large right tail confirms that volatility is a material feature of this portfolio.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
Other risk-related segments


Bonus score, fuel type, and circulation area show visible loss-ratio differences.
These segments are screening candidates, not final causal conclusions.


Bonus score, fuel type, and circulation area all show visible differences in aggregate loss ratio. These are useful candidates for underwriting or pricing review.

Brand-level screen


Upper-right brands combine higher claim frequency and higher loss ratio.
Larger bubbles should be prioritised because they represent more exposure.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
Implications

Review premium adequacy for comprehensive products.
Investigate 2024 deterioration in loss ratio.
Use bonus score, fuel type, and circulation area as segmentation checks.
Examine extreme losses separately from typical-policy behaviour.
Validate any pricing action with exposure and mix-adjusted modelling.


The visual analytics process identifies where to investigate next. It does not replace actuarial modelling, but it provides a clear evidence trail for prioritising portfolio questions.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5.1: Building Ternary Plot with R
text:
pacman::p_load(plotly, ggtern, tidyverse)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.width = 8, fig.height = 7, out.width = "100%")


#Reading the data into R environment
pop_data <- read_csv("../data/r4va/respopagsex2000to2018_tidy.csv")


#Deriving the young, economy active and old measures
agpop_mutated <- pop_data %>%
  mutate(`Year` = as.character(Year))%>%
  spread(AG, Population) %>%
  mutate(YOUNG = rowSums(.[4:8]))%>%
  mutate(ACTIVE = rowSums(.[9:16]))  %>%
  mutate(OLD = rowSums(.[17:21])) %>%
  mutate(TOTAL = rowSums(.[22:24])) %>%
  filter(Year == 2018)%>%
  filter(TOTAL > 0)


#Building the static ternary plot
ggtern(data=agpop_mutated,aes(x=YOUNG,y=ACTIVE, z=OLD)) +
  geom_point()









#Building the static ternary plot
ggtern(data=agpop_mutated, aes(x=YOUNG,y=ACTIVE, z=OLD)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title="Population structure, 2018") +
  theme_rgbw()









# reusable function for creating annotation object
label <- function(txt) {
  list(
    text = txt, 
    x = 0.5, y = 1.08,
    ax = 0, ay = 0,
    xref = "paper", yref = "paper",
    xanchor = "center",
    align = "center",
    font = list(family = "serif", size = 15, color = "white"),
    bgcolor = "#b3b3b3", bordercolor = "black", borderwidth = 2
  )
}

# reusable function for axis formatting
axis <- function(txt) {
  list(
    title = txt, tickformat = ".0%", tickfont = list(size = 10)
  )
}

ternaryAxes <- list(
  aaxis = axis("Young"), 
  baxis = axis("Active"), 
  caxis = axis("Old")
)

# Initiating a plotly visualization 
plot_ly(
  agpop_mutated, 
  a = ~YOUNG, 
  b = ~ACTIVE, 
  c = ~OLD, 
  color = I("black"), 
  type = "scatterternary"
) %>%
  layout(
    annotations = label("Ternary Markers"), 
    ternary = ternaryAxes,
    width = 750,
    height = 650,
    margin = list(l = 20, r = 20, b = 20, t = 80)
  )

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics for Data Discovery
text:
This report applies visual analytics to a real-world motor insurance portfolio from a Spanish non-life insurer. The exercise brief asks for R-based visual analytics that go beyond dashboard reporting and help discover factors linked to portfolio profitability and volatility.
The report is organised in the following structure: context first, analytical sandbox, data preparation, univariate exploration, bivariate analysis, statistical validation, and final findings. The analysis uses the Mendeley motor portfolio data.
Two analytical definitions are used throughout the report:

Profitability is measured by aggregate profit = total_premium - total_incurred and by aggregate loss_ratio = total_incurred / total_premium. Lower loss ratio indicates better underwriting profitability before expenses.
Volatility is measured by claim occurrence, claim frequency, capped individual loss ratio, high-loss policy rate, and upper-tail loss-ratio behaviour.

The main question is: which portfolio segments show weaker profitability or higher volatility, and are those patterns visually and statistically defensible?

Bivariate analysis compares profitability and volatility across time and major risk-related segments. It builds on the Section 3 finding that the portfolio is zero-inflated at policy level but exposed to a small positive-loss tail, especially through liability_incurred and other incurred-cost components. The comparisons use the data dictionary meaning of each segment: coverage structure, claims-history quality, billing frequency, fuel type, circulation area, driver/vehicle characteristics, and exposure-adjusted claim outcomes.

Claim frequency also rises slightly from 0.302 to 0.312, while the high-loss policy share increases from 8.0% to 9.7%.
This pattern links the Section 3 positive-loss tail to a time trend: 2024 is not only larger in exposure, but also more loss-heavy.

4.3 Segment scan: bonus score, fuel type, and circulation area


Show the code
overall_loss_ratio <- sum(motor$total_incurred, na.rm = TRUE) / sum(motor$total_premium, na.rm = TRUE)

seg_long <- bind_rows(
  portfolio_summary(motor, bonus_score) |>
    mutate(segment = "Bonus score", category = as.character(bonus_score)),
  portfolio_summary(motor, fuel_type) |>
    mutate(segment = "Fuel type", category = fct_na_value_to_level(as.factor(fuel_type), "Missing") |> as.character()),
  portfolio_summary(motor, circulation_area) |>
    mutate(segment = "Circulation area", category = as.character(circulation_area)),
  portfolio_summary(motor, payment_frequency) |>
    mutate(segment = "Payment frequency", category = as.character(payment_frequency))
)

seg_long |>
  mutate(
    category = fct_reorder(category, loss_ratio),
    label = paste0(pct(loss_ratio), " | exp ", comma(round(exposure)))
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = loss_ratio, y = category)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = overall_loss_ratio, linewidth = 0.8, colour = "#08519c") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8, colour = "red") +
  geom_segment(aes(x = overall_loss_ratio, xend = loss_ratio, yend = category), colour = "grey75") +
  geom_point(aes(size = exposure, colour = segment), alpha = 0.82, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = label), hjust = -0.05, size = 2.7, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    labels = pct,
    limits = c(0, max(seg_long$loss_ratio, overall_loss_ratio, 1, na.rm = TRUE) * 1.30)
  ) +
  scale_size_continuous(labels = comma, range = c(2.8, 7.5)) +
  facet_wrap(~ segment, scales = "free_y") +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  labs(
    title = "Loss ratio differs across risk-related categories",
    subtitle = "Blue line marks the overall portfolio loss ratio; red dashed line marks 100% break-even before expenses.",
    x = "Aggregate loss ratio",
    y = NULL,
    size = "Exposure"
  ) +
  theme(plot.margin = margin(5.5, 55, 5.5, 5.5))










Observations

Non-good bonus scores show weaker experience: neutral N and poor-history B have loss ratios of about 81.4% and 79.0%, compared with 69.7% for favourable-history G.
Diesel vehicles (D) have a higher loss ratio than gasoline vehicles (G), about 73.0% versus 64.3%.
Urban circulation areas (U) have a higher loss ratio than rural areas (R), about 71.4% versus 68.9%.
Semi-annual (S) and quarterly (Q) payment frequencies have higher loss ratios than annual (A) payment, so billing pattern is a useful screening variable.
The dot-plot labels add total exposure, making it easier to separate materially important categories from small or sparse categories.
These visual signals are not causal by themselves because exposure, product mix, vehicle profile, and policy type can differ across segments.

The heatmap links the year-level deterioration with policy-type differences.
COMP_N, comprehensive without excess, is the clearest 2024 hotspot, with a loss ratio slightly above break-even at about 102.4%.
COMP_N worsens from 72.8% in 2022 to 92.3% in 2023 and 102.4% in 2024, suggesting persistent deterioration rather than a one-year isolated cell.
COMP_E, comprehensive with excess, also rises in 2024, reinforcing that comprehensive-cover segments should be monitored separately from third-party-focused covers such as TP and TPG.

The bubble chart screens brands by claim frequency, loss ratio, and exposure.
Upper-right brands combine higher claim frequency and higher loss ratio, so they represent volatility candidates rather than automatically poor brands; brand can proxy vehicle profile, repair cost, parts availability, and theft attractiveness.
Among brands with exposure at least 1,000, Mitsubishi and Mazda have the highest aggregate loss ratios, about 99.8% and 93.9% respectively.
Large upper-right bubbles should be prioritised for deeper investigation because they combine underwriting impact with enough exposure to matter.




4.6 Statistical validation
The dataset is large and skewed, so visual signals are validated with non-parametric and categorical tests:

Kruskal-Wallis tests check whether capped individual loss ratio differs across segment groups.
Chi-square tests check whether claim occurrence differs across segment groups.
Spearman correlations check monotonic relationships between numerical variables and capped loss ratio.



Show the code

    variable = v,
    statistic = unname(kt$statistic),
    p_value = kt$p.value
  )
})

chi_tbl <- map_dfr(test_vars, \(v) {

  tibble(
    test = "Chi-square",
    variable = v,
    statistic = unname(ct$statistic),
    p_value = ct$p.value
  )

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics for Data Discovery
text:
5 Key findings
The objective of this report is to use visual analytics to identify portfolio segments associated with weaker underwriting profitability and higher volatility. The main findings are:

The portfolio is profitable overall, but the margin is exposed to loss volatility. Across 354,140 policy-year records, the portfolio generates about EUR31.2 million underwriting profit before expenses and an aggregate loss ratio of about 70.3%. However, only about 14.3% of records have claims, so profitability is sensitive to a relatively small claim-producing tail.
Profitability deteriorates in 2024. The aggregate loss ratio increases from about 65.6% in 2022 and 66.5% in 2023 to about 74.7% in 2024. This indicates that incurred losses are growing faster than premium and that the latest year should be treated as an early-warning period.
Policy type is the strongest and most defensible segmentation signal. Comprehensive covers have materially weaker results than third-party-focused covers. COMP_N has the highest aggregate loss ratio at about 93.9%, and the year-by-policy heatmap shows COMP_N exceeding break-even in 2024 at about 102.4%.
Secondary segment variables explain where profitability and volatility are concentrated. Non-good bonus scores, diesel vehicles, urban circulation areas, and shorter payment frequencies show higher loss ratios than their comparison groups. These are useful underwriting screening variables, but they should be interpreted together with exposure and policy mix.
Volatility is concentrated in claim frequency and upper-tail outcomes rather than in the typical policy-year record. Boxplots, capped loss-ratio distributions, policy-type comparisons, and brand-level bubbles show that most records remain low-loss, while a smaller set of claim-heavy segments drives the high-loss tail.
The visual signals are statistically supported but not causal. Kruskal-Wallis and chi-square tests support group differences across key segmentation variables. Because the dataset is large and observational, the results should guide deeper underwriting investigation rather than be used as standalone pricing rules.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics for Data Discovery
text:
6 Recommendations

Prioritise comprehensive-cover review. Monitor COMP_N and COMP_E separately from the rest of the portfolio, with particular attention to 2024 COMP_N performance. Review claim frequency, claim severity, excess structure, and premium adequacy before making portfolio-wide pricing changes.
Use 2024 as an early-warning trigger. Build a recurring year-by-segment loss-ratio monitor so that deterioration by policy type, bonus score, fuel type, circulation area, and payment frequency is detected before it becomes an aggregate profitability issue.
Apply segment screening, not automatic repricing. Treat high-loss brand, diesel, urban, non-good bonus-score, and shorter-payment-frequency groups as candidates for deeper review. Validate whether the observed differences remain after controlling for exposure, policy type, vehicle age, driver age, and claim mix.
Strengthen volatility management. Track high-loss policy rate, claim frequency, severity, and capped loss ratio in addition to aggregate loss ratio. These measures align better with the report objective because they reveal tail-risk segments hidden by portfolio-level profitability.
Enrich the portfolio data before final underwriting action. Add external geography, traffic-density, weather, theft-risk, and vehicle repair-cost indicators to explain why specific segments underperform and to separate true risk effects from product-mix effects.

text:
This report applies visual analytics to a real-world motor insurance portfolio from a Spanish non-life insurer. The exercise brief asks for R-based visual analytics that go beyond dashboard reporting and help discover factors linked to portfolio profitability and volatility.
The report is organised in the following structure: context first, analytical sandbox, data preparation, univariate exploration, bivariate analysis, statistical validation, and final findings. The analysis uses the Mendeley motor portfolio data.
Two analytical definitions are used throughout the report:

Profitability is measured by aggregate profit = total_premium - total_incurred and by aggregate loss_ratio = total_incurred / total_premium. Lower loss ratio indicates better underwriting profitability before expenses.
Volatility is measured by claim occurrence, claim frequency, capped individual loss ratio, high-loss policy rate, and upper-tail loss-ratio behaviour.

The main question is: which portfolio segments show weaker profitability or higher volatility, and are those patterns visually and statistically defensible?

3 Task 1: Univariate visual analytics
This section applies the recommended univariate visual for each source column in the motor insurance portfolio. The approach is type-specific:

identifiers are summarised with uniqueness and duplicate counts, not plotted as continuous numbers;
categorical variables use count/composition bars, with top-N grouping for high-cardinality fields;
ordinary numerical variables use a histogram plus boxplot;
optional premium and incurred-loss variables are split into zero-versus-positive bars plus positive-value distributions;
claim counts use count bars and a separate 0-claim versus 1-or-more-claims view.

3.2 Reusable profiling functions

format_profile_value <- function(x, var = NULL) {
  if (length(x) == 0 || is.na(x) || !is.finite(x)) return("NA")
  if (!is.null(var) && str_detect(var, "premium|incurred|vehicle_value|profit|severity")) {
    return(money(x))
  }
  comma(round(x, 2))
}

numeric_profile_summary <- function(df, var) {
  x <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(df[[var]]))
  finite_x <- x[is.finite(x)]
  tibble(
    metric = c("Missing records", "Missing share", "Zero share", "Minimum", "Median", "Mean", "95th percentile", "Maximum"),
    value = c(
      comma(sum(is.na(x))),
      pct(mean(is.na(x))),
      if (length(finite_x) == 0) "NA" else pct(mean(finite_x == 0)),
      if (length(finite_x) == 0) "NA" else format_profile_value(min(finite_x), var),
      if (length(finite_x) == 0) "NA" else format_profile_value(median(finite_x), var),
      if (length(finite_x) == 0) "NA" else format_profile_value(mean(finite_x), var),
      if (length(finite_x) == 0) "NA" else format_profile_value(quantile(finite_x, 0.95, na.rm = TRUE), var),
      if (length(finite_x) == 0) "NA" else format_profile_value(max(finite_x), var)
    )
  )
}

categorical_profile_summary <- function(df, var) {
  x <- df[[var]]
  non_missing <- x[!is.na(x)]
  tab <- sort(table(non_missing), decreasing = TRUE)
  tibble(
    metric = c("Missing records", "Missing share", "Distinct non-missing values", "Top category", "Top-category share"),
    value = c(
      comma(sum(is.na(x))),
      pct(mean(is.na(x))),
      comma(n_distinct(x, na.rm = TRUE)),
      if (length(tab) == 0) "NA" else names(tab)[1],
      if (length(tab) == 0) "NA" else pct(as.numeric(tab[1]) / length(non_missing))
    )
  )
}

id_profile_summary <- function(df, var) {
  x <- df[[var]]
  tibble(
    metric = c("Policy-year records", "Unique IDs", "Duplicate ID records", "Missing ID records"),
    value = c(
      comma(length(x)),
      comma(n_distinct(x, na.rm = TRUE)),
      comma(length(x) - n_distinct(x, na.rm = TRUE)),
      comma(sum(is.na(x)))
    )
  )
}

profile_summary <- function(df, var, family) {
  if (family == "id") return(id_profile_summary(df, var))
  if (family %in% c("categorical", "ordinal", "year")) return(categorical_profile_summary(df, var))
  numeric_profile_summary(df, var)
}

empty_plot <- function(title, message) {
  ggplot() +
    annotate("text", x = 0, y = 0, label = message) +
    theme_void() +
    labs(title = title)
}

hist_box_visual <- function(df, var, title = NULL, subtitle = NULL, positive_only = FALSE, log_scale = FALSE) {
  plot_df <- tibble(value = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(df[[var]]))) |>
    filter(is.finite(value))
  if (positive_only) plot_df <- plot_df |> filter(value > 0)

  if (nrow(plot_df) == 0) {
    return(empty_plot(paste("Distribution of", var), "No finite values available"))
  }

  if (!log_scale) {
    lower <- quantile(plot_df$value, 0.01, na.rm = TRUE)
    upper <- quantile(plot_df$value, 0.99, na.rm = TRUE)
    plot_df <- plot_df |>
      mutate(value_plot = pmin(pmax(value, lower), upper))
    plot_subtitle <- coalesce(subtitle, "Histogram and boxplot; values are capped at the 1st and 99th percentiles for readability only.")
  } else {
    plot_df <- plot_df |> mutate(value_plot = value)
    plot_subtitle <- coalesce(subtitle, "Positive values only; x-axis is log-scaled to reveal skewed claim-cost severity.")
  }

  x_labeller <- if (str_detect(var, "premium|incurred|vehicle_value|profit|severity")) money else comma

  hist <- ggplot(plot_df, aes(x = value_plot)) +
    geom_histogram(bins = 35, colour = "white", fill = "#2c7fb8") +
    labs(x = var, y = "Number of records") +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = x_labeller)

  box <- ggplot(plot_df, aes(x = value_plot, y = "")) +
    geom_boxplot(fill = "#a6bddb", colour = "#045a8d", outlier.alpha = 0.35) +
    labs(x = var, y = NULL) +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = x_labeller)

  if (log_scale) {
    hist <- hist + scale_x_log10(labels = x_labeller)
    box <- box + scale_x_log10(labels = x_labeller)
  }

  hist / box +
    plot_layout(heights = c(3, 1)) +
    plot_annotation(
      title = coalesce(title, paste("Distribution of", var)),
      subtitle = plot_subtitle
    )
}

zero_positive_bar <- function(df, var, positive_label = "Positive") {
  fill_values <- c("#bdbdbd", "#2c7fb8", "#fdae6b", "#756bb1")
  names(fill_values) <- c("Zero", positive_label, "Negative", "Missing")

  tibble(value = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(df[[var]]))) |>
    mutate(status = case_when(
      is.na(value) ~ "Missing",
      value > 0 ~ positive_label,
      value == 0 ~ "Zero",
      TRUE ~ "Negative"
    )) |>
    count(status, name = "n") |>
    mutate(
      share = n / sum(n),
      status = factor(status, levels = c("Zero", positive_label, "Negative", "Missing"))
    ) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = status, y = share, fill = status)) +
    geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
    geom_text(aes(label = percent(share, accuracy = 0.1)), vjust = -0.25, size = 3.5) +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = percent, limits = c(0, NA)) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = fill_values) +
    labs(
      title = paste("Zero versus positive", var),
      x = NULL,
      y = "Share of records"
    )
}

      positive_only = TRUE,

}

claim_count_visual <- function(df, var) {
  count_plot <- tibble(value = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(df[[var]]))) |>
    mutate(claim_count = if_else(is.na(value), "Missing", as.character(value))) |>
    count(claim_count, name = "n") |>
    mutate(claim_count = fct_reorder(claim_count, suppressWarnings(as.numeric(claim_count)), .na_rm = TRUE)) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = claim_count, y = n)) +
    geom_col(fill = "#2c7fb8") +
    labs(
      title = paste("Claim-count distribution for", var),
      x = "Claim count",
      y = "Number of records"
    )

  flag_plot <- tibble(value = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(df[[var]]))) |>
    mutate(status = case_when(
      is.na(value) ~ "Missing",
      value == 0 ~ "0 claims",
      value > 0 ~ "1 or more claims",
      TRUE ~ "Negative"
    )) |>
    count(status, name = "n") |>
    mutate(
      share = n / sum(n),
      status = factor(status, levels = c("0 claims", "1 or more claims", "Negative", "Missing"))
    ) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = status, y = share, fill = status)) +
    geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
    geom_text(aes(label = percent(share, accuracy = 0.1)), vjust = -0.25, size = 3.5) +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = percent, limits = c(0, NA)) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("0 claims" = "#bdbdbd", "1 or more claims" = "#2c7fb8", "Negative" = "#fdae6b", "Missing" = "#756bb1")) +
    labs(
      title = paste("Claim occurrence for", var),
      x = NULL,
      y = "Share of records"
    )

  count_plot / flag_plot + plot_layout(heights = c(1.4, 1))
}

year_visual <- function(df, var) {
  df |>
    transmute(year_value = fct_na_value_to_level(as.factor(.data[[var]]), level = "Missing")) |>
    count(year_value, name = "n") |>
    ggplot(aes(x = year_value, y = n, group = 1)) +
    geom_col(fill = "#756bb1", alpha = 0.75) +
    geom_line(colour = "#d95f0e", linewidth = 1) +
    geom_point(colour = "#d95f0e", size = 2) +
    labs(
      title = "Policy-year record counts by year",
      x = "Year",
      y = "Number of records"

categorical_visual <- function(df, var, family = "categorical", top_n = NA_real_) {
  plot_df <- df |>
    transmute(category = fct_na_value_to_level(as.factor(.data[[var]]), level = "Missing")) |>
    count(category, name = "n")

  if (family == "ordinal" && var == "bonus_score") {
    preferred_levels <- c("bad", "Bad", "neutral", "Neutral", "good", "Good")
    level_order <- c(intersect(preferred_levels, as.character(plot_df$category)), setdiff(as.character(plot_df$category), preferred_levels))
    plot_df <- plot_df |> mutate(category = factor(as.character(category), levels = level_order))
  } else {
    if (!is.na(top_n)) {
      plot_df <- plot_df |>
        mutate(category = fct_lump_n(category, n = top_n, w = n, other_level = "Other")) |>
        group_by(category) |>
        summarise(n = sum(n), .groups = "drop")
    }
    plot_df <- plot_df |> mutate(category = fct_reorder(category, n))
  }

  plot_df |>
    mutate(share = n / sum(n)) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = category, y = share)) +
    geom_col(fill = "#756bb1") +
    coord_flip() +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) +
    labs(
      title = paste("Composition of", var),
      subtitle = if (!is.na(top_n)) paste("Top", top_n, "categories retained; remaining categories grouped as Other.") else "Bars show share of policy-year records.",
      x = NULL,
      y = "Share of records"
    )
}

make_profile_visual <- function(df, spec_row) {
  var <- spec_row$variable
  family <- spec_row$visual_family
  top_n <- spec_row$top_n

  if (family == "id") return(NULL)
  if (family == "year") return(year_visual(df, var))
  if (family %in% c("categorical", "ordinal")) return(categorical_visual(df, var, family, top_n))
  if (family == "discrete") return(categorical_visual(df, var, "categorical", NA_real_))
  if (family == "optional_premium") return(optional_premium_visual(df, var))
  if (family == "incurred") return(incurred_visual(df, var))
  if (family == "claim_count") return(claim_count_visual(df, var))
  hist_box_visual(df, var)
}

profile_insights <- function(df, spec_row) {
  var <- spec_row$variable
  family <- spec_row$visual_family
  x <- df[[var]]
  bullets <- c(paste0("Recommended check: ", spec_row$what_to_look_for))

  if (family == "id") {
    duplicate_records <- length(x) - n_distinct(x, na.rm = TRUE)
    bullets <- c(
      bullets,
      paste0("There are ", comma(n_distinct(x, na.rm = TRUE)), " unique IDs across ", comma(length(x)), " policy-year records."),
      paste0("Duplicate ID records equal ", comma(duplicate_records), "; this is expected if an insured appears in more than one year, but the ID should not be modelled as a continuous value.")
    )
    return(paste0("- ", bullets, collapse = "\n") |> paste0("\n"))
  }

  if (family %in% c("categorical", "ordinal", "year", "discrete")) {
    tab <- sort(table(x, useNA = "no"), decreasing = TRUE)
    missing_share <- mean(is.na(x))
    distinct_values <- n_distinct(x, na.rm = TRUE)
    if (missing_share > 0) bullets <- c(bullets, paste0("Missing records account for ", pct(missing_share), " and are shown explicitly where relevant."))
    if (distinct_values > 20) bullets <- c(bullets, paste0("The variable has ", distinct_values, " distinct values, so top-N grouping protects readability."))
    if (length(tab) > 0) bullets <- c(bullets, paste0("The largest category is `", names(tab)[1], "` with ", pct(as.numeric(tab[1]) / sum(tab)), " of non-missing records."))
  } else {
    num_x <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(x))
    finite_x <- num_x[is.finite(num_x)]
    if (length(finite_x) == 0) bullets <- c(bullets, "No finite values are available for interpretation.")
    if (length(finite_x) > 0) {
      missing_share <- mean(is.na(num_x))
      zero_share <- mean(finite_x == 0)
      median_value <- median(finite_x)
      mean_value <- mean(finite_x)
      p95_value <- quantile(finite_x, 0.95, na.rm = TRUE)
      max_value <- max(finite_x)
      if (missing_share > 0) bullets <- c(bullets, paste0("Missing records account for ", pct(missing_share), "."))
      if (zero_share > 0.50) bullets <- c(bullets, paste0("The variable is zero-inflated: ", pct(zero_share), " of finite records are zero."))
      if (median_value == 0 && p95_value > 0) {
        bullets <- c(bullets, "The median is zero but the upper tail is positive, so the positive-value visual is more informative than a standard histogram alone.")
      } else if (abs(mean_value) > abs(median_value) * 2 && p95_value > median_value) {
        bullets <- c(bullets, "The mean is much larger than the median, indicating right skew and possible expensive outliers.")
      }
      bullets <- c(bullets, paste0("The 95th percentile is ", format_profile_value(p95_value, var), " and the maximum is ", format_profile_value(max_value, var), "."))
    }
  }

  if (length(bullets) > 3) bullets <- bullets[1:3]
  paste0("- ", bullets, collapse = "\n") |> paste0("\n")
}

The dataset is large and skewed, so visual signals are validated with non-parametric and categorical tests:

Kruskal-Wallis tests check whether capped individual loss ratio differs across segment groups.
Chi-square tests check whether claim occurrence differs across segment groups.
Spearman correlations check monotonic relationships between numerical variables and capped loss ratio.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics for Data Discovery
text:
5 Key findings

The portfolio is profitable in aggregate but exposed to a claim-driven upper tail. Most records have no claim, but a minority of claim records strongly affects incurred loss and loss ratio.
Profitability weakens in 2024. The year-level loss ratio increases, showing that incurred losses grew faster than premium.
Policy type is the clearest segmentation signal. COMP_N and COMP_E have higher loss ratios than third-party-focused products, suggesting that comprehensive cover requires closer pricing and claim review.
Bonus score, fuel type, circulation area, and payment frequency show meaningful differences. These variables help explain portfolio heterogeneity, but each should be interpreted together with exposure and product mix.
Volatility is concentrated in tails, not medians. Boxplots, capped loss-ratio charts, and the brand bubble chart show why underwriting decisions should account for high-loss policy-year behaviour.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics for Data Discovery
text:
6 Recommendations

Monitor COMP_N and COMP_E separately from the rest of the portfolio because their loss-ratio and volatility profile differs materially.
Use the 2024 deterioration as an early-warning signal and review whether it is caused by exposure growth, claim frequency, severity, or a changing product mix.
Treat high-loss brand, fuel, and circulation-area segments as screening candidates for deeper underwriting review rather than as immediate pricing rules.
Extend the analysis with external enrichment, such as regional traffic density, weather exposure, or vehicle repair-cost indicators, to better explain the root causes of underperformance.

Part 1: Network data with tidygraph, ggraph, and visNetwork
This section uses the GAStech email data. The nodes file contains employee information, while the edges file contains email communication records.

1.1 Load R packages

pacman::p_load(
  igraph, tidygraph, ggraph,
  visNetwork, lubridate, clock,
  tidyverse, graphlayouts,
  concaveman, ggforce
)

The main packages are:

tidygraph for creating and manipulating graph objects.
ggraph for static network visualisation.
visNetwork for interactive network visualisation.
lubridate for handling dates.



1.2 Import network data

network_data_dir <- "../data/r4va/chap27"

GAStech_nodes <- read_csv(file.path(network_data_dir, "GAStech_email_node.csv"))
GAStech_edges <- read_csv(file.path(network_data_dir, "GAStech_email_edge-v2.csv"))

The nodes table describes the employees. The edges table records who sent email to whom, together with the date, time, subject, and email labels.

glimpse(GAStech_edges)

The first check is to inspect the data structure. In the raw data, SentDate is usually imported as character, so it must be converted before weekday analysis.


1.3 Prepare date and weekday fields

GAStech_edges <- GAStech_edges %>%
  mutate(SendDate = dmy(SentDate)) %>%
  mutate(Weekday = wday(
    SentDate,
    label = TRUE,
    abbr = FALSE
  ))

dmy() converts the date string into a proper date. wday() extracts the weekday so that email patterns can be compared across days.


1.4 Aggregate email links

GAStech_edges_aggregated <- GAStech_edges %>%
  filter(MainSubject == "Work related") %>%
  group_by(source, target, Weekday) %>%
  summarise(Weight = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  filter(source != target) %>%
  filter(Weight > 1)

The raw edge data contains one row per email. For network visualisation, the emails are aggregated by sender, receiver, and weekday. Weight shows how many emails were sent for each relationship.


1.5 Create a tidygraph object

GAStech_graph <- tbl_graph(
  nodes = GAStech_nodes,
  edges = GAStech_edges_aggregated,
  directed = TRUE
)

GAStech_graph

A tbl_graph stores the node table and edge table together. Since email has a sender and receiver, the graph is directed.

GAStech_graph %>%
  activate(edges) %>%
  arrange(desc(Weight))

Sorting the edges by Weight helps identify stronger communication links.


1.6 Basic static network graph

ggraph(GAStech_graph) +
  geom_edge_link() +
  geom_node_point()

This first graph shows the basic network structure. The layout is simple and is mainly used to check whether the graph has been created correctly.

g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph) +
  geom_edge_link(aes()) +
  geom_node_point(aes())

g + theme_graph()

theme_graph() removes unnecessary chart elements and gives the network plot a cleaner appearance.

g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph) +
  geom_edge_link(aes(colour = "grey50")) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = "grey40"))

g + theme_graph(
  background = "grey10",
  text_colour = "white"
)

The colour and background can be adjusted to improve contrast.


1.7 Improve layout and visual encoding

g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph, layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(aes()) +
  geom_node_point(aes())

g + theme_graph()

The Fruchterman-Reingold layout places connected nodes closer together.

g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph, layout = "nicely") +
  geom_edge_link(aes()) +
  geom_node_point(aes(
    colour = Department,
    size = 3
  ))

g + theme_graph()

Colouring nodes by department makes it easier to see whether communication is concentrated within or across departments.

g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph, layout = "nicely") +
  geom_edge_link(
    aes(width = Weight),
    alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(
    aes(colour = Department),
    size = 3
  )

g + theme_graph()

Edge width is mapped to email frequency. Thicker edges represent stronger communication links.


1.8 Facet network graphs

set_graph_style()

g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph, layout = "nicely") +
  geom_edge_link(
    aes(width = Weight),
    alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(
    aes(colour = Department),
    size = 2
  )

g + facet_edges(~Weekday)

Faceting by weekday allows daily communication patterns to be compared.

set_graph_style()

g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph, layout = "nicely") +
  geom_edge_link(
    aes(width = Weight),
    alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(
    aes(colour = Department),
    size = 2
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

g + facet_edges(~Weekday)

Moving the legend to the bottom makes the small multiples easier to read.

set_graph_style()

g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph, layout = "nicely") +
  geom_edge_link(
    aes(width = Weight),
    alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(
    aes(colour = Department),
    size = 2
  )

g + facet_edges(~Weekday) +
  th_foreground(
    foreground = "grey80",
    border = TRUE
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

The foreground panel border makes each weekday panel clearer.

set_graph_style()

g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph, layout = "nicely") +
  geom_edge_link(
    aes(width = Weight),
    alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(
    aes(colour = Department),
    size = 2
  )

g + facet_nodes(~Department) +
  th_foreground(
    foreground = "grey80",
    border = TRUE
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

Faceting by department separates the employees into groups and helps identify department-level communication patterns.


1.9 Add network measures

g <- GAStech_graph %>%
  mutate(betweenness_centrality = centrality_betweenness()) %>%
  ggraph(layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(
    aes(width = Weight),
    alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(
    colour = Department,
    size = betweenness_centrality
  ))

g + theme_graph()

Betweenness centrality highlights employees who sit between other employees in the communication network. Larger nodes are more important connectors.

g <- GAStech_graph %>%
  ggraph(layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(
    aes(width = Weight),
    alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(
    colour = Department,
    size = centrality_betweenness()
  ))

g + theme_graph()

The same measure can also be calculated directly inside the plot aesthetic.


1.10 Detect communities

g <- GAStech_graph %>%
  mutate(community = as.factor(
    group_edge_betweenness(
      weights = Weight,
      directed = TRUE
    )
  )) %>%
  ggraph(layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(
    aes(width = Weight),
    alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = community))

g + theme_graph()

Community detection groups employees who are more closely connected to each other.

g <- GAStech_graph %>%
  activate(nodes) %>%
  mutate(
    community = as.factor(group_optimal(weights = Weight)),
    betweenness_measure = centrality_betweenness()
  ) %>%
  ggraph(layout = "fr") +
  geom_mark_hull(
    aes(
      x, y,
      group = community,
      fill = community
    ),
    alpha = 0.2,
    expand = unit(0.3, "cm"),
    radius = unit(0.3, "cm")
  ) +
  geom_edge_link(
    aes(width = Weight),
    alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(
    aes(
      fill = Department,
      size = betweenness_measure
    ),
    color = "black",
    shape = 21
  )

g + theme_graph()

The hulls show the detected communities. Node size still represents betweenness centrality.


1.11 Create an interactive network
visNetwork uses different edge column names. The edge table is rebuilt with from, to, and weight.

GAStech_edges_vis <- GAStech_edges %>%
  left_join(GAStech_nodes, by = c("sourceLabel" = "label")) %>%
  rename(from = id) %>%
  left_join(GAStech_nodes, by = c("targetLabel" = "label")) %>%
  rename(to = id) %>%
  filter(MainSubject == "Work related") %>%
  group_by(from, to) %>%
  summarise(weight = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  filter(from != to) %>%
  filter(weight > 1)


visNetwork(GAStech_nodes, GAStech_edges_vis)

This creates a basic interactive graph.

visNetwork(GAStech_nodes, GAStech_edges_vis) %>%
  visIgraphLayout(layout = "layout_with_fr")

The layout can be improved by using an igraph layout algorithm.

GAStech_nodes_vis <- GAStech_nodes %>%
  rename(group = Department)

visNetwork(GAStech_nodes_vis, GAStech_edges_vis) %>%
  visIgraphLayout(layout = "layout_with_fr") %>%
  visLegend() %>%
  visLayout(randomSeed = 123)

The group column controls node colour, and the legend explains the department colours.

visNetwork(GAStech_nodes_vis, GAStech_edges_vis) %>%
  visIgraphLayout(layout = "layout_with_fr") %>%
  visEdges(
    arrows = "to",
    smooth = list(
      enabled = TRUE,
      type = "curvedCW"
    )
  ) %>%
  visLegend() %>%
  visLayout(randomSeed = 123)

Arrows show the direction of emails.

visNetwork(GAStech_nodes_vis, GAStech_edges_vis) %>%
  visIgraphLayout(layout = "layout_with_fr") %>%
  visOptions(
    highlightNearest = TRUE,
    nodesIdSelection = TRUE
  ) %>%
  visLegend() %>%
  visLayout(randomSeed = 123)

highlightNearest and nodesIdSelection make the graph easier to explore interactively.

title: Hands-on Exercise 7: Network and Text Visualisation with R
text:
Part 2: Text data with tidytext
This section uses text documents from the 20 Newsgroups dataset. The workflow imports many text files, cleans the text, tokenises words, calculates TF-IDF, and builds a bigram network.

2.1 Load R packages

pacman::p_load(
  tidytext, widyr, wordcloud, DT, ggwordcloud,
  textplot, lubridate, hms, tidyverse,
  tidygraph, ggraph, igraph
)



2.2 Import many text files

news20 <- "../data/r4va/chap29/20news/"

The folder should contain one subfolder per newsgroup. Each subfolder contains individual text files.

read_folder <- function(infolder) {
  tibble(file = dir(infolder, full.names = TRUE)) %>%
    mutate(text = map(file, read_lines)) %>%
    transmute(
      id = basename(file),
      text
    ) %>%
    unnest(text)
}

This helper function reads all files in one folder and returns a tidy data frame.

raw_text <- tibble(folder = dir(news20, full.names = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(folder_out = map(folder, read_folder)) %>%
  unnest(cols = c(folder_out)) %>%
  transmute(
    newsgroup = basename(folder),
    id,
    text
  )

write_rds(raw_text, "../data/r4va/news20.rds")

The result has one row per line of text. The newsgroup column records which group the message belongs to.


2.3 Explore message counts

raw_text %>%
  group_by(newsgroup) %>%
  summarise(messages = n_distinct(id), .groups = "drop") %>%
  ggplot(aes(messages, newsgroup)) +
  geom_col(fill = "lightblue") +
  labs(
    x = "Number of messages",
    y = NULL
  )

This bar chart checks whether the groups have similar or different numbers of messages.


2.4 Clean the text

cleaned_text <- raw_text %>%
  group_by(newsgroup, id) %>%
  filter(
    cumsum(text == "") > 0,
    cumsum(str_detect(text, "^--")) == 0
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

This step removes email headers and lines after automated signatures.

cleaned_text <- cleaned_text %>%
  filter(
    str_detect(text, "^[^>]+[A-Za-z\\d]") | text == "",
    !str_detect(text, "writes(:|\\.\\.\\.)$"),
    !str_detect(text, "^In article <")
  )

This step removes quoted replies and other repeated email text.


2.5 Tokenise words

usenet_words <- cleaned_text %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, text) %>%
  filter(
    str_detect(word, "[a-z']$"),
    !word %in% stop_words$word
  )

unnest_tokens() splits text into one word per row. Stop words such as common articles and connectors are removed.

usenet_words %>%
  count(word, sort = TRUE)

This count shows the most frequent remaining words.


2.6 Visualise words

words_by_newsgroup <- usenet_words %>%
  count(newsgroup, word, sort = TRUE) %>%
  ungroup()


wordcloud(
  words_by_newsgroup$word,
  words_by_newsgroup$n,
  max.words = 300
)

The word cloud gives a quick overview of frequent words.

set.seed(1234)

words_by_newsgroup %>%
  filter(n > 0) %>%
  ggplot(aes(
    label = word,
    size = n
  )) +
  geom_text_wordcloud() +
  theme_minimal() +
  facet_wrap(~newsgroup)

Faceting the word cloud by newsgroup makes group-level differences easier to compare.


2.7 Calculate TF-IDF

tf_idf <- words_by_newsgroup %>%
  bind_tf_idf(word, newsgroup, n) %>%
  arrange(desc(tf_idf))

TF-IDF gives higher scores to words that are common in one newsgroup but less common in others.

DT::datatable(tf_idf, filter = "top") %>%
  formatRound(
    columns = c("tf", "idf", "tf_idf"),
    digits = 3
  ) %>%
  formatStyle(
    0,
    target = "row",
    lineHeight = "25%"
  )

An interactive table is useful for searching and checking TF-IDF values.

tf_idf %>%
  filter(str_detect(newsgroup, "^sci\\.")) %>%
  group_by(newsgroup) %>%
  slice_max(tf_idf, n = 12) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(word = reorder(word, tf_idf)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(
    tf_idf,
    word,
    fill = newsgroup
  )) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~newsgroup,
    scales = "free"
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "tf-idf",
    y = NULL
  )

This plot highlights the most distinctive terms in science-related newsgroups.


2.8 Correlate words across groups

newsgroup_cors <- words_by_newsgroup %>%
  pairwise_cor(
    newsgroup,
    word,
    n,
    sort = TRUE
  )

Word correlation shows which newsgroups use similar vocabularies.

set.seed(2017)

newsgroup_cors %>%
  filter(correlation > 0.025) %>%
  graph_from_data_frame() %>%
  ggraph(layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(
    alpha = correlation,
    width = correlation
  )) +
  geom_node_point(
    size = 6,
    color = "lightblue"
  ) +
  geom_node_text(
    aes(label = name),
    color = "red",
    repel = TRUE
  ) +
  theme_void()

The graph connects newsgroups with similar word usage.


2.9 Work with bigrams

bigrams <- cleaned_text %>%
  unnest_tokens(
    bigram,
    text,
    token = "ngrams",
    n = 2
  )

bigrams

A bigram is a pair of consecutive words. Bigrams help show common phrases, not just single words.

bigrams_count <- bigrams %>%
  filter(bigram != "NA") %>%
  count(bigram, sort = TRUE)

bigrams_count

This identifies the most common word pairs.

bigrams_separated <- bigrams %>%
  filter(bigram != "NA") %>%
  separate(
    bigram,
    c("word1", "word2"),
    sep = " "
  )

bigrams_filtered <- bigrams_separated %>%
  filter(!word1 %in% stop_words$word) %>%
  filter(!word2 %in% stop_words$word)

bigrams_filtered

The bigram is split into two columns so that stop words can be removed from both positions.


2.10 Build a bigram network

bigram_counts <- bigrams_filtered %>%
  count(word1, word2, sort = TRUE)


bigram_graph <- bigram_counts %>%
  filter(n > 3) %>%
  graph_from_data_frame()

bigram_graph

The bigram graph treats words as nodes and common word pairs as directed edges.

set.seed(1234)

ggraph(bigram_graph, layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link() +
  geom_node_point() +
  geom_node_text(
    aes(label = name),
    vjust = 1,
    hjust = 1
  )

This first network shows the basic bigram structure.

set.seed(1234)

a <- grid::arrow(
  type = "closed",
  length = unit(0.15, "inches")
)

ggraph(bigram_graph, layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(
    aes(edge_alpha = n),
    show.legend = FALSE,
    arrow = a,
    end_cap = circle(0.07, "inches")
  ) +
  geom_node_point(
    color = "lightblue",
    size = 5
  ) +
  geom_node_text(
    aes(label = name),
    vjust = 1,
    hjust = 1
  ) +
  theme_void()

Arrows show word order, and edge transparency shows how frequently each bigram appears.

title: Take-home Exercise 2: VAST Mini-Challenge 1
text:
This report builds a visual analytics workflow for VAST Challenge 2026 Mini-Challenge 1. The case asks whether TenantThread’s inappropriate pre-embargo release of the CivicLoom merger was a deliberate leak or a system breakdown under crisis pressure.
The analysis uses the internal communications, public FleX posts, agent deliberations, and environmental context recorded in MC1_final_00.json.
The working conclusion is:






Important



The release was not an accidental one-message failure. The records show an intentional early-release sequence after SaltWind published the merger story at 5:00 PM. Legal-Agent and Social-Manager-Agent reframed the 6:00 PM embargo as moot, claimed CivicLoom verbal consent, instructed PR-Intern to publish, and amplified the merger from personal and anonymous accounts before 6:00 PM. However, the system also broke down structurally: Judge warnings were exceeded, personal/anonymous channels were not controlled, and sentiment/market-survival logic displaced embargo enforcement.


Important evidence limitation: the dataset contains agent communications. It records Legal-Agent’s claim that CivicLoom verbal consent was obtained, but it does not independently verify that consent.

text:
2 Analytical sandbox


Show the code
library(tidyverse)
library(jsonlite)
library(lubridate)
library(plotly)
library(DT)
library(igraph)
library(scales)

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))

`%||%` <- function(x, y) {
  if (is.null(x) || length(x) == 0) y else x
}

collapse_text <- function(x) {
  if (is.null(x) || length(x) == 0) return("")
  if (is.list(x)) x <- unlist(x, recursive = TRUE, use.names = FALSE)
  paste(as.character(x), collapse = " | ")
}

mc1_file <- if (file.exists("TH_Ex/data/th_ex2/raw/MC1_final_00.json")) {
  "TH_Ex/data/th_ex2/raw/MC1_final_00.json"
} else {
  "data/th_ex2/raw/MC1_final_00.json"
}
mc1_raw <- jsonlite::read_json(mc1_file, simplifyVector = FALSE)



2.1 Extract rounds and communications


Show the code
rounds <- map2_dfr(mc1_raw$rounds, seq_along(mc1_raw$rounds), function(r, i) {
  ec <- r$environment_context
  tibble(
    round_id = i,
    hour = ymd_hms(r$hour),
    headline = collapse_text(ec$event_headline),
    narrative = collapse_text(ec$event_narrative),
    media_events = collapse_text(ec$media_events),
    external_actions = collapse_text(ec$external_actor_actions),
    social_alerts = collapse_text(ec$social_manager_alerts),
    critical_deadlines = collapse_text(ec$critical_deadlines),
    agents_unavailable = collapse_text(ec$agents_unavailable),
    n_messages = length(r$communications),
    n_participants = length(r$participants)
  )
})

communications <- map2_dfr(mc1_raw$rounds, seq_along(mc1_raw$rounds), function(r, round_id) {
  map2_dfr(r$communications, seq_along(r$communications), function(c, message_order) {
    state <- c$internal_state %||% list()
    tibble(
      round_id = round_id,
      message_order = message_order,
      message_id = collapse_text(c$message_id),
      timestamp = ymd_hms(c$timestamp),
      agent_id = collapse_text(c$agent_id),
      agent_role = collapse_text(c$agent_role),
      agent_label = collapse_text(c$agent_label),
      channel = collapse_text(c$channel),
      recipients = list(as.character(unlist(c$recipients %||% character(), recursive = TRUE, use.names = FALSE))),
      recipients_text = collapse_text(c$recipients),
      message_type = collapse_text(c$message_type),
      responding_to = collapse_text(c$responding_to),
      reacting = collapse_text(state$reacting),
      rationalizing = collapse_text(state$rationalizing),
      deliberating = collapse_text(state$deliberating),
      content = collapse_text(c$content)
    )
  })
}) %>%
  mutate(
    date = as_date(timestamp),
    period = case_when(
      timestamp < ymd_hms("2046-06-05 00:00:00") ~ "Prior period",
      timestamp < ymd_hms("2046-06-05 17:00:00") ~ "Crisis day before SaltWind merger story",
      timestamp < ymd_hms("2046-06-05 18:00:00") ~ "Post-SaltWind / pre-embargo-lift",
      TRUE ~ "After embargo lift"
    ),
    public_channel = channel %in% c("official_post", "personal_post", "anonymous_post"),
    side_channel = channel %in% c("side_huddle", "one_on_one_chat"),
    official_channel = channel %in% c("comms_huddle", "official_post"),
    text_all = str_c(content, reacting, rationalizing, deliberating, sep = " "),
    embargo_keyword = str_detect(str_to_lower(content), "civicloom|harborcrest|residentedge|merger|6pm|6 pm|announcement|rebrand"),
    compliance_keyword = str_detect(str_to_lower(text_all), "judge|embargo|compliance|10b-5|outside counsel|pslra|safe harbor"),
    market_pressure_keyword = str_detect(str_to_lower(text_all), "stock|mac|covenant|sentiment|arr|surviv|breach|market"),
    public_embargo_signal = public_channel & embargo_keyword
  )

participants <- map2_dfr(mc1_raw$rounds, seq_along(mc1_raw$rounds), function(r, round_id) {
  map_dfr(r$participants, function(p) {
    meta <- p$agent_round_metadata %||% list()
    tibble(
      round_id = round_id,
      agent_id = collapse_text(p$agent_id),
      agent_role = collapse_text(p$agent_role),
      agent_label = collapse_text(p$agent_label),
      declared_action = collapse_text(p$declared_action),
      sentiment_at_turn = collapse_text(meta$sentiment_at_turn),
      action_classification = collapse_text(meta$action_classification)
    )
  })
}) %>%
  left_join(rounds %>% select(round_id, hour), by = "round_id")

summary_counts <- tibble(
  metric = c("Rounds", "Communications", "Public FleX posts", "Public posts containing embargo terms", "Agents"),
  value = c(
    nrow(rounds),
    nrow(communications),
    sum(communications$public_channel),
    sum(communications$public_embargo_signal),
    n_distinct(communications$agent_label)
  )
)

DT::datatable(summary_counts, rownames = FALSE, options = list(dom = "t", pageLength = 10))

Known substantive risk: tenant analytics misuse and re-identification risk were already recognized internally before the crisis day.
Embargoed strategic dependency: the CivicLoom merger became the preferred survival path after revenue, client, and sentiment pressure worsened.
Control erosion: Judge was installed after the Elena incident, but agents still used side huddles, personal posts, anonymous posts, and market-survival arguments.
Early-release decision: after SaltWind published at 5:00 PM, Legal-Agent claimed bilateral consent, issued GO at 5:19 PM, and Legal/Social-Manager public posts named CivicLoom and HarborCrest before the 6:00 PM embargo lift.

5 Leading indicators
The following risk index is not a ground-truth compliance score. It is a visual analytic proxy built from observable signals: embargo-term mentions, public embargo-term posts, side-channel volume, compliance references, and market-pressure language.

  geom_line(colour = "#2166ac") +

ggplotly(p_risk, tooltip = "text")







5.1 Leading indicators found

May 29 Elena incident: a personal post linked TenantThread leadership with CivicLoom leadership before the embargo lift. This was the clearest prior warning.
Persistent side-channel coordination: side huddles and one-on-one chats were repeatedly used to stage public responses outside the main compliance-visible channel.
Aggregation exposure: Judge explicitly warned at 3:08 PM that official, personal, and anonymous accounts had reached the maximum tolerable threshold.
Market-survival language: agents repeatedly framed silence as causing MAC breach, covenant breach, stock collapse, and deal death. This language became a justification layer for relaxing embargo discipline.
Public-domain rationalization: by 5:00 PM, agents argued that SaltWind and anonymous posts had already made the deal public, reducing the perceived cost of self-announcement.

8 Other occasions with release-like behavior
The final release was new in severity, but not new in pattern. Similar behavior appeared earlier in weaker forms:

Personal-account signaling: the May 29 Elena incident and June 5 Legal/Social personal posts both used personal FleX accounts to add signal outside formal corporate release controls.
Anonymous amplification: Legal-Agent used anonymous posts to defend TenantThread’s narrative; this bypassed ordinary attribution while still shaping public interpretation.
Aggregation logic: agents repeatedly argued that because public fragments already existed, additional statements only matched the market’s inference. Judge identified this as aggregation exposure before the final release.
Speed over review: PR-Intern was repeatedly instructed to publish within 60 seconds of a GO signal, reducing time for compliance review.
Market-survival framing: stock, MAC, covenant, and sentiment models were used as decision authority, often stronger than embargo policy itself.

section: 9 Why the prior occasions did not produce noticeable action
text:
9 Why the prior occasions did not produce noticeable action
Prior deviations did not force stronger corrective action because each was explainable in isolation:

Ambiguity: early signals were vague (big things coming, strategic developments) rather than explicit deal terms.
Deletion and deniability: the Elena post was deleted quickly and could be called unauthorized personal activity.
Channel blind spots: Judge was added to Comms Huddle, but side huddles, one-on-one chats, personal accounts, and anonymous posts remained active.
Competing crisis goals: market survival, client retention, and hostile media response created a continuous argument for faster public action.
Aggregation tolerance: the team began treating inferred public knowledge as permission to add slightly more signal.
No single catastrophic earlier post: earlier actions did not combine direct counterparty naming, official/personal amplification, and timestamped governance framing in one sequence. The June 5 5:19–5:54 PM window did.

section: 10 Findings and answer to the Mini-Challenge questions
text:
10 Findings and answer to the Mini-Challenge questions

10.1 What key events and relationships led to the inappropriate release?
The release followed a causal chain from known analytics misuse, to external exposés, to a merger-dependent survival strategy, to a compliance near miss, to crisis-day market pressure. Legal-Agent and Social-Manager-Agent became the main decision and amplification actors. PR-Intern was positioned as the official publishing executor. Judge-Agent provided a clear warning at 3:08 PM, but the later GO sequence at 5:19 PM overrode the spirit of that warning.


10.2 How does the release behavior compare with typical behavior?
Typical behavior was internal deliberation plus carefully framed governance communications. Release behavior was different: fast, public, multi-channel, and counterparty-specific. Legal and Social-Manager used personal and anonymous posts as operational release channels before the scheduled 6:00 PM lift.


10.3 Were there leading indicators?
Yes. The Elena post, the side-channel coordination pattern, the repeated market-survival framing, the Judge aggregation warning, and the growing use of public timestamp narratives were all leading indicators.


10.4 Prior occasions where actual behavior differed from expected behavior
The strongest prior cases were the May 29 Elena post, post-Judge side-channel venting, the 1:00 PM oversight gap on June 5, and the 3:20 PM official strategic-partnership statement after Judge’s aggregation concern.


10.5 Other occasions with behavior like the release
The system had already shown personal-account signaling, anonymous amplification, rapid PR-Intern execution, and aggregate-disclosure rationalization. The final breach combined these patterns at higher intensity.


10.6 Why did prior occasions not result in noticeable action?
Because each earlier deviation was partial, deniable, or not direct enough to trigger a public consequence. The control response was also incomplete: Judge was added as a monitor, but channel governance and personal/anonymous posting authority were not actually constrained.

title: Take-home Exercise 2: VAST Mini-Challenge 1
text:
11 Final judgement
TenantThread’s team did not simply suffer a random automation malfunction. The inappropriate release was a deliberate early-release sequence under pressure, rationalized by SaltWind’s 5:00 PM story and by Legal-Agent’s claim of CivicLoom verbal consent. The larger failure was systemic: compliance enforcement did not control all channels, the agents optimized for market narrative recovery, and prior near misses were treated as manageable rather than as evidence that the release system could evade the embargo.
